passage: Jyoti, a customer asks when her lehenga will be ready, and you say "Tuesday" just to please her. I did that too, at twenty-four, when I'd just opened this shop. Then I missed three weddings' worth of Tuesdays. So I started doing what my Abbu did with his carpentry orders. I opened my old register and looked: how long did the last five bridal lehengas actually take? Not how long I hoped. Eleven days, fourteen, nine, sixteen, twelve. Then I broke the work into parts: cutting, embroidery, lining, fitting. And I added three days for the things that always go wrong, like the thread shop being shut or the customer changing the neckline. After that, people started saying "Rehana's dates are real dates." So take the register. Look first, then promise.

qa.q: How long did the last five bridal lehengas take?
qa.a: Eleven days, fourteen, nine, sixteen and twelve.

qa.q: Why did Rehana start checking the old register?
qa.a: After missing three weddings' worth of Tuesdays, Rehana wanted dates based on what had really happened, not on hope.

qa.q: What steps does Rehana want Jyoti to follow before promising a date?
qa.a: Check the register for similar orders, break the job into parts, add days for what usually goes wrong, and only then give a date.

qa.a: Customers could plan their weddings with confidence, trusting that a promised date would really be met.

passage: The client call was in ten minutes, and Mehak leaned over Disha's desk. "They want the new menu screens for their ordering app. Can we promise Friday?" Disha felt the pull to say yes; the team had been praised all week. Instead she opened the project log. "The last two sets of screens like this took eight and eleven working days," she said. "Design, review, the client's changes, then fixes. Each step slipped at least once." She sketched the four parts on a sticky note, gave each a number of days, and added two more for the client's usual round of edits. "Realistically, the Thursday after next. I'd rather promise that and deliver early." Mehak exhaled. "They won't love it." "They'll love a missed Friday less." Mehak took the sticky note into the call.

passage: In a Ludhiana housing society, Rajni Aunty wanted her kitchen redone before Diwali. "Five weeks, beta, can you do it?" Jasleen, twenty-five and three years into running her small interiors firm, didn't answer straight away. She scrolled to the notes she kept on every job: the Malhotras' kitchen, seven weeks; the Batras', six and a half; both held up by marble delivery. She walked the kitchen with a tape measure and listed each stage on the back of a catalogue: breaking, plumbing, marble, cabinets, painting, cleaning. Next to marble she wrote "plus one week, always." "Honestly, Aunty, seven weeks. If we start Monday, it's done a week before Diwali, not the night before." Rajni Aunty frowned, then nodded. "Better than half a kitchen on Diwali."

Ritu looked up from her laptop at her brother. "Zubin, before I say yes, give me two minutes."
"Two minutes to say yes?"
"To check." She opened a spreadsheet. "Last three small websites. The bakery: I guessed four days, it took nine. The yoga studio: guessed five, took eight. The tailor: guessed three, took seven, because the photos came late."
Zubin leaned over. "Okay, that's… a lot."
"So I break it down. Menu page, photos, contact form, mobile check, his changes. And I add a few days for surprises." She typed. "Realistic date: the Friday after next."
"He'll be disappointed."
"Less disappointed than if I promise this Friday and miss it."
Zubin nodded slowly and picked up his phone to call his friend.

When I started my own carpentry workshop in Nashik, I made the classic mistake: I promised the first customer, Kishore sir, his wardrobe "in ten days." It took twenty-three. He was polite about it, but I could see he'd stopped trusting my dates.
I'm Ujjwal, and the change came from an old notebook. My father, also a carpenter, left me, his only son, a notebook where he had written every job for years: what it was, the date promised, the date finished. Almost every line ran late.
So I started my own notebook. Now, when someone asks for a date, I look back at similar jobs. I break the work into parts: wood from the market, cutting, polishing, fitting. I add a week for surprises like rain delaying the polish.
Last month Kishore sir came back for a bookshelf. I said five weeks. It was ready in four and a half. He smiled and said, "You've changed, beta."

qa.a: It took twenty-three days.

qa.a: He noticed that Kishore sir had stopped trusting his dates, even though Kishore sir was polite about it.

qa.a: Kishore sir seems pleased and reassured, since he can trust Ujjwal's dates again, as his smile and 'You've changed' show.

passage:
Tuesday
Nitin asked me today when the annual report would be ready. My mouth wanted to say "two weeks." It always wants to say two weeks. Instead I said, "Let me check and tell you tomorrow."
So tonight I opened my old calendar. Last year's report: started 3 Feb, finished 19 March. Six and a half weeks. The year before: seven. Both times I had promised two.
Broke it into pieces: data from four departments (always late, so a week), writing (two weeks), charts (a week), two rounds of edits (a week each, because Nitin always adds a section). That's six weeks, plus one for surprises.
Tomorrow I'll tell him seven weeks. He won't love it. But I'd rather disappoint him once on Wednesday than every Friday after.
Minakshi

passage: The block office in Sindhudurg wanted a date. "When will the new toilet block at the Kudal school be ready?" the officer asked Pallavi. Dear Pallavi,

Thank you for asking us to redesign your restaurant's menu and signage. You asked if we could finish in two weeks.

I'd love to say yes. But before promising, I looked at our last five similar projects. On average, they took five weeks. The fastest took three. Each one had printing delays and at least one round of changes we didn't expect.

So here is what I'd suggest. I've broken the job into four parts: design ideas (one week), your feedback (one week), final artwork (one week), printing and fitting (one week). I've added a one-week buffer for the unexpected.

That makes five weeks. I know it's longer than you hoped. But I'd rather give you a date I can keep than one I'll miss.

If two weeks is essential, we could do the menu first and signage later.

Warm regards,
Mridul

qa.a: On average, they took five weeks.

qa.q: What does Mridul seem to feel about promising two weeks?
qa.a: Mridul seems tempted to say yes but cautious, preferring an honest date over one likely to be missed.

qa.q: What makes Mridul's estimate reliable?
qa.a: Mridul checked how long similar projects actually took, broke the job into parts and added a buffer before promising a date.

passage:
You asked how I stopped missing deadlines, Samir? I'm Lavanya, and I used to miss every single one.

My old way: someone asked how long, and I'd imagine myself working perfectly, no interruptions, no mistakes. "Three days," I'd say. It always took eight.

Now I do three things.

First, I look back. How long did the last similar report actually take? I keep a little log now, so I know. Usually, about twice what I'd guess.

Second, I break it into pieces. Research, draft, review, fixes. Each piece gets its own time. That shows me parts I forgot.

Third, I add a buffer. Not a huge one. Maybe a third extra.

Then I give a date. My manager was surprised the first time I said "ten days" instead of "three". But I delivered on day nine.

It feels less impressive. But people trust my dates now. That's worth more.

qa.q: How long did Lavanya's old three-day estimates actually take?
qa.a: It always took eight.

qa.q: How does Lavanya feel about giving longer estimates now?
qa.a: Lavanya feels it is less impressive but is proud and relieved that people now trust the dates.

qa.q: Which of Lavanya's three steps would help most, and why?
qa.a: Looking back at how long similar tasks really took helps most, because it replaces the hopeful picture with real evidence.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's manager see the new estimates?
qa.a: The manager was surprised at first but likely trusts Lavanya more now that dates are met.

grounding: A mature worker estimates from past tasks, breaks work into pieces and adds a buffer before promising dates.

When the municipal officer asked for a finish date, the contractor said "three weeks" straight away. Pradeep didn't answer. He opened a folder of old repair records.

"Seven weeks," he said. The officer frowned. The contractor muttered.

It took six and a half. I don't know exactly what Pradeep felt, but he didn't look surprised at all.
